# Requirement #2283: Generator and analyzer must report MsgPack004 for an unkeyed member of a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2283

#### Bug description

Both `MessagePackGenerator` and `MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer` silently ignore an unkeyed public member on a **closed generic value type defined in a referenced assembly** when that type is used as a member of a `[MessagePackObject]` type. The consuming project builds cleanly and generates a resolver, but the unkeyed member is omitted from serialization. This is only a runtime failure, so trimmed and NativeAOT apps can ship broken for releases before anyone notices. The analyzer should report `MsgPack004` in the consuming project at the usage of the closed generic type, even though the member itself is declared in metadata.

#### Repro steps

Two projects. `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack;
namespace Lib;

[MessagePackObject]
public partial record struct Item<T>([property: Key(0)] string Key)
{
    public int Unkeyed { get; init; }
}
```

`app`, with a `ProjectReference` to `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack; using Lib;
namespace App;

[MessagePackObject]
public sealed partial record Cmd([property: Key(0)] string Scope)
{
    [Key(1)] public Item<int> Member { get; init; }
}
```

Then `dotnet build` on `app`. Both projects are in the attached `mp-repro.zip`.

#### Expected behavior

A build with a generated resolver in `app` and a `MsgPack004` diagnostic in `app` pointing at the `Item<int>` member, so the missing key on `Item<int>.Unkeyed` is caught in the consuming project.

#### Actual behavior

The build succeeds with no diagnostic. `app.dll` contains `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`, but `Item<int>.Unkeyed` is not serialized. The analyzer does not report `MsgPack004` because the member is declared in metadata and the diagnostic is dropped.

- Version used: MessagePack 3.1.8
- Runtime: .NET 10 (SDK 10.0.204), Windows 11

#### Additional context

**What triggers it.** `Item` is declared in `lib`, `Cmd` in `app`:

| `Item` declared as | result |
|---|---|
| `record struct Item<T>` with unkeyed member | **no diagnostic** |
| `struct Item<T>` with unkeyed member | **no diagnostic** |
| `struct Item` with unkeyed member | `MsgPack004` |
| `record struct Item` with unkeyed member | `MsgPack004` |
| `class Item<T>` with unkeyed member | `MsgPack004` |
| `record class Item<T>` with unkeyed member | `MsgPack004` |

So it needs all three of: **generic**, **value type**, **from a referenced assembly**. Moving the identical `Item<T>` declaration into `app` itself makes the diagnostic appear, which is what makes this specific to metadata symbols.

**Stack trace.**

```
None. The analyzer returns without reporting a diagnostic.
```

**Workaround.** Putting `[MessagePackFormatter(typeof(ItemFormatter<>))]` on the generic value type avoids the need for a key, at the cost of hand-writing the formatter. Adding `[Key(1)]` to `Unkeyed` in `lib` also works when `lib` is under your control.

**Possibly related:** #2092 reports CS8785 from the v3 generator, but with a different inner exception and no repro.

requirement_points.text: When a [MessagePackObject] type has a member whose type is a closed generic value type (struct or record struct) declared in a referenced assembly, the source generator completes without throwing IndexOutOfRangeException (no CS8785).
Under the same conditions, the MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer completes without throwing IndexOutOfRangeException (no AD0001).
The consuming assembly still receives a generated MessagePack resolver (such as GeneratedMessagePackResolver) instead of silently producing none.
Diagnostics about members of a type defined in a referenced assembly are not reported in the consuming compilation; they are left to the assembly that defines the type.
The fix covers both plain generic structs and generic record structs coming from metadata.

plants.description: GetPropertyIdentifierLocation indexes DeclaringSyntaxReferences with [0] instead of FirstOrDefault(). For a property that comes from metadata (a referenced assembly) the collection is empty, so this throws IndexOutOfRangeException again and the generator/analyzer fail with CS8785/AD0001.

The MemberNeedsKey diagnostic uses First() instead of FirstOrDefault() when locating the member. Members of types that come from metadata have no DeclaringSyntaxReferences, so First() throws and the analyzer crashes with AD0001.

The null check on reportAnalyzerDiagnostic is dropped, so in the source generator (where no diagnostic reporter is supplied) reportDiagnostic becomes a non-null delegate wrapping a null callback. Any diagnostic raised then dereferences the null callback and the generator fails with CS8785, leaving the assembly with no generated resolver.

The location filter now also accepts Location.None, which is exactly the location that diagnostics about metadata members get. Diagnostics about members of a type defined in a referenced assembly are therefore reported in the consuming compilation, which is what the requirement says must not happen.

The diagnostic reporter is wired up without the ReportIfLocatedInCompilation wrapper, so the metadata-location filtering is gone entirely and diagnostics about members declared in a referenced assembly are reported in the consuming compilation.

The guard inside ReportIfLocatedInCompilation is removed and every diagnostic is forwarded, so diagnostics whose location is not in the compilation being analyzed (i.e. about types and members from referenced assemblies) are reported in the consuming compilation again.

The metadata-safe lookup for the property location is replaced with First(), which throws when the property has no declaration in source. The crash that the change was meant to remove comes back for members of types declared in a referenced assembly.
The MemberNeedsKey diagnostic indexes DeclaringSyntaxReferences directly instead of using the safe lookup, so the analyzer throws again for members that come from metadata rather than source.
The conditional is written with the positive test and the branches swapped; behaviour is identical.
Location.IsInSource is exactly equivalent to Location.SourceTree being non-null, so the guard reads the same way but behaves identically.
Parameter renamed; the body uses the new name and no behaviour changes.
Only parentheses are added around the null-conditional expression; the null propagation is unchanged.
